lead: A gate cannot switch instantly: its output node carries a load capacitance C<sub>L</sub>, and the transistors can supply only a limited current. The propagation delay is the time from the input crossing its 50% level to the output crossing its 50% level. Every clock period, setup check and timing report is built from these delays, so this chapter defines t<sub>PHL</sub>, t<sub>PLH</sub>, t<sub>p</sub>, rise time and fall time, gives two hand estimates that agree, and lists what makes up C<sub>L</sub>.
prereq: You need: the saturation current of a MOSFET (see MOSFET I-V characteristics) and the CMOS inverter.

items: t<sub>PHL</sub>, output high-to-low: from the input crossing V<sub>DD</sub>/2 rising to the output crossing V<sub>DD</sub>/2 falling. The nMOS pull-down sets it.
t<sub>PLH</sub>, output low-to-high: from the input crossing V<sub>DD</sub>/2 falling to the output crossing V<sub>DD</sub>/2 rising. The pMOS pull-up sets it.
t<sub>p</sub> = (t<sub>PHL</sub> + t<sub>PLH</sub>)/2, the single number used for a gate in a path.
t<sub>f</sub> and t<sub>r</sub>, fall and rise times: the output alone moving between 90% and 10% of V<sub>DD</sub> (some books use 80% and 20%).

blocks.text: Delay and edge time answer different questions. Delay says when the edge arrives; rise or fall time says how sharp it is. A slow edge at the input of the next gate makes that gate slower and wastes short-circuit power, so timing tools track both.
A ring oscillator, an odd number N of inverters in a loop, makes these numbers measurable on silicon. Each edge travels round the ring twice per period, so its frequency is f = 1/(2Nt<sub>p</sub>).

Average current. For tPHL the output must lose the charge CLVDD/2 to reach the 50% point. With an input step, the nMOS is saturated while Vout > VDD − Vtn and linear below that, where its current is a little smaller. Using the saturation current for the whole half swing gives:
tPHL ≈ CLVDD/(2IDsat), IDsat = (kn/2)(VDD − Vtn)² Here cL is in farads, VDD in volts and IDsat in amperes, giving seconds. tPLH uses the pMOS current (kp/2)(VDD − |Vtp|)² the same way.

RC model. Replace the on transistor by a resistance Req. A step into an RC circuit reaches 50% after ln 2 × ReqCL, so tp = 0.69ReqCL, and its 10% to 90% time is ln 9 × ReqCL = 2.2ReqCL. A fair Req is the average of the transistor's V/I over the half swing: about (3/4)VDD/IDsat. With that Req the RC delay is 0.69 × 0.75 = 0.52 CLVDD/IDsat, within 4% of the average-current estimate. Neither is exact; simulation is the reference, and the computed waveform in Figure 3.3.1 shows how close both come.

blocks.text: Either way, delay grows with C<sub>L</sub> and V<sub>DD</sub> and falls with transistor width. Raising V<sub>DD</sub> still makes the gate faster, because current grows roughly as the square of the overdrive while the charge grows only linearly.

C<sub>L</sub> is the sum of the driver's own drain diffusion capacitances (nMOS and pMOS), the gate-drain overlaps, the wire, and the gate capacitance of every fan-out input, C<sub>in</sub> ≈ C<sub>ox</sub>(W<sub>n</sub>L<sub>n</sub> + W<sub>p</sub>L<sub>p</sub>). Doubling the fan-out roughly doubles C<sub>L</sub> and so the delay.

The gate-drain capacitance Cgd joins input and output, which swing in opposite directions. During a transition the voltage across it changes by about twice the swing, so it counts roughly twice (the Miller effect). Long wires add capacitance and resistance; their models are in interconnect parameters.
Sizing trades these against each other: a wider driver gives more current but loads the stage before it. The chapter on logical effort finds the best balance.

examples.question: A CMOS inverter drives C<sub>L</sub> = 50 fF at V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V. The nMOS has k<sub>n</sub> = 200 µA/V², V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.5 V; the pMOS has k<sub>p</sub> = 80 µA/V², |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.5 V. Estimate t<sub>PHL</sub>, t<sub>PLH</sub> and t<sub>p</sub>. What k<sub>p</sub> would make the edges equal?
steps: Charge to remove: C<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub>/2 = 50 fF × 0.9 V = 45 fC. t<sub>PHL</sub> = 45 fC / 169 µA = 0.266 ns.
pMOS: I = (80/2)(1.3)² = 67.6 µA, so t<sub>PLH</sub> = 45 fC / 67.6 µA = 0.666 ns.
Equal edges need equal currents, k<sub>p</sub> = k<sub>n</sub> = 200 µA/V², a pMOS 200/80 = 2.5 times wider.
Check with the step response of the square-law nMOS, integrated numerically: the output leaves saturation at 1.3 V after 0.148 ns and crosses 0.9 V at 0.270 ns, 1.5% above the estimate.
examples.answer: t<sub>PHL</sub> ≈ 0.27 ns, t<sub>PLH</sub> ≈ 0.67 ns, t<sub>p</sub> ≈ 0.47 ns; widening the pMOS 2.5 times balances them at about 0.27 ns each.

examples.question: For the nMOS of the first example find R<sub>eq</sub>, the RC estimate of t<sub>PHL</sub> and the RC estimate of the fall time.
steps: t<sub>PHL</sub> ≈ 0.69 × 8.0 kΩ × 50 fF = 0.276 ns, 4% above the average-current value of 0.266 ns.
The numerical step response gives a 90% to 10% fall of 0.59 ns: the transistor discharges the top of the swing at a constant current, faster than an exponential, so the RC fall time is pessimistic.
examples.answer: R<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 8.0 kΩ, t<sub>PHL</sub> ≈ 0.28 ns; the RC model gives t<sub>f</sub> ≈ 0.88 ns against 0.59 ns from the device equations.

traps: Swapping t<sub>PHL</sub> and t<sub>PLH</sub>. t<sub>PHL</sub> is the output falling, set by the nMOS and caused by a rising input.
Dropping the 2 in C<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub>/(2I<sub>Dsat</sub>). Delay ends at the 50% point, so only half the swing is moved.
Squaring V<sub>DD</sub> instead of the overdrive V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub> in the saturation current.
Calling rise time a delay. Rise time is measured on the output alone; delay is from input to output.
Unit slips: fF × V = fC and fC ÷ µA = ns. Keep fF with µA and read nanoseconds.

quiz.q: Define t<sub>PHL</sub> and name the transistor that sets it.
quiz.a: The time from the input crossing V<sub>DD</sub>/2 rising to the output crossing V<sub>DD</sub>/2 falling. The nMOS pull-down sets it.

quiz.q: Between which levels are rise and fall times usually measured?
quiz.a: 10% and 90% of V<sub>DD</sub>; some texts use 20% and 80%, so state the levels you use.

quiz.q: C<sub>L</sub> doubles while the transistors stay the same. What happens to t<sub>PHL</sub>?
quiz.a: It doubles: the current is unchanged and the charge C<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub>/2 doubles.

quiz.q: An nMOS with I<sub>Dsat</sub> = 200 µA drives C<sub>L</sub> = 80 fF at V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V. Estimate t<sub>PHL</sub>.
quiz.a: Charge = 80 fF × 0.9 V = 72 fC; t<sub>PHL</sub> = 72 fC / 200 µA = 0.36 ns.

quiz.q: A ring oscillator of 101 inverters runs at 25 MHz. Find the inverter delay.
Why does C<sub>gd</sub> load a switching input more than its static value?
quiz.a: Input and output move in opposite directions, so the voltage across C<sub>gd</sub> changes by about twice the input swing and it draws about twice the charge (the Miller effect).

quiz.q: A designer doubles only the pMOS width of an inverter. Discuss the effect on t<sub>PLH</sub>, t<sub>PHL</sub>, t<sub>p</sub> and the input capacitance.
quiz.a: t<sub>PLH</sub> roughly halves because the pull-up current doubles. t<sub>PHL</sub> rises slightly because the bigger pMOS adds drain capacitance to C<sub>L</sub>. t<sub>p</sub> improves by less than the t<sub>PLH</sub> gain. The input capacitance grows, slowing the stage that drives this inverter, so pMOS width is chosen to balance the two edges, not maximised.

beyond: Not for the exam. Sign-off timing does not use these formulas: a static timing analyser looks up each cell's delay and output slew in a Liberty table indexed by input slew and load, at several process, voltage and temperature corners. In nanometre processes the wire resistance and crosstalk between neighbours often matter more than the gate itself. Search next for static timing analysis, Liberty timing tables and PVT corners.

figure.caption: The output of the example inverter after an input step at 0.1 ns, computed from the nMOS equations. It falls at a constant rate while the nMOS is saturated, then more slowly, and crosses 0.9 V 0.27 ns after the step.

spec.aria: Plot of voltage against time: the input steps from 0 to 1.8 volts at 0.1 nanoseconds; the output falls from 1.8 volts, leaves saturation at 1.3 volts, and crosses 0.9 volts 0.27 nanoseconds after the step.
